gap: No result ChatGPT got states that a suitcase's built-in charge controller is only for 12 V batteries: to charge a portable power station, ACOPOWER says to skip the controller and plug the panel's own cables into the station's solar cable.
standout_why: ChatGPT's answer lists 'Portable power station (Jackery, EcoFlow, Bluetti)' as a use but never says the controller has to be bypassed for one. Its 13 results are Renogy's own pages (the 100/200W suitcase page under several URLs, the STCS100D-VOY20 manual, and the 220/400W and 300W suitcases) plus one Outbound Power reseller listing. I couldn't fully check those pages. Renogy's product pages and outboundpower.com returned HTTP 429 every time. The cited manual and the Renogy CDN copy of the STCS200D-VOY20 manual were 1-page PDFs with no readable text. So the score of 2 assumes the Renogy suitcase pages don't already say this. They might.
decides: This splits the pick by what the shopper charges. For a bare 12 V battery (AGM, flooded or LiFePO4), a suitcase with a built-in controller is the right buy, and ACOPOWER's 20A controller lists 8 battery types including LiFePO4 and LTO and auto-detects 12 V or 24 V. For a power station (Dealectric lists BLUETTI, ALLPOWERS, EcoFlow, Jackery and Anker SOLIX), the controller goes unused because the station has its own. In that case a plain panel, or a panel-plus-station kit like the ALLPOWERS SP037 or BLUETTI kits, is the better buy than a controller suitcase.
